questions.question: A sportswear brand plans an online flash sale that it expects will triple orders for one weekend. Which channel activity should it coordinate with the sale?

options.B: Reduce the number of products available online
options.C: Cancel orders placed during the weekend
options.D: Arrange extra warehouse and shipping capacity

questions.explanation: Arrange extra warehouse and shipping capacity. A promotion that triples orders requires the channel, including warehouses and shipping partners, to handle the extra volume. Arranging extra staff and shipping capacity helps orders arrive on time, protecting customer satisfaction. Canceling orders, reducing products available and pausing promotion would all undermine the sale. When promotion and distribution aren't coordinated, a successful campaign can turn into a wave of late deliveries and complaints that damage the brand. Some brands also share inventory plans with influencers and partners before big sales.

performanceIndicator.text: Coordinate channel management with other marketing activities

questions.question: A small hot-sauce maker can't afford to sell to thousands of stores directly, so it sells cases to a food wholesaler. What is the main benefit of this arrangement for the hot-sauce maker?

options.A: The wholesaler sets the sauce's recipe
options.B: The maker no longer needs to produce sauce
options.C: The wholesaler reaches many stores efficiently
options.D: Consumers pay less than the maker's cost

questions.explanation: The wholesaler reaches many stores efficiently. Wholesalers buy large quantities from producers and resell them to many retailers, which saves small producers the time and cost of selling to each store individually. The maker still produces the sauce and controls the recipe, so those choices are wrong. Consumers won't pay less than the maker's cost, since every channel member must earn a profit. In exchange for these services, the maker sells to the wholesaler at a lower price than it would charge stores directly, a trade-off many small producers find worthwhile.

performanceIndicator.text: Explain the nature of channels of distribution

questions.question: A client asks a research firm to remove survey responses that criticize the client's product before the results are shared with investors. Which of the following is the most ethical response:

options.B: Remove the negative responses as requested
options.C: Change the negative answers to positive ones
options.D: Share only the most favorable results

questions.explanation: Report all valid responses accurately. Marketing research is useful only when it is honest. Removing, changing or selectively reporting responses would give investors a false picture of how customers view the product, which is unethical and could be fraud. The firm should report all valid responses accurately and can help the client understand the criticism and how to address it. Researchers who manipulate results risk their professional reputation, and decisions based on distorted research often lead to costly mistakes.

performanceIndicator.text: Explain the role of ethics in marketing-information management

questions.question: Which of the following is an advantage of online video ads compared with newspaper ads:

options.A: They can show products in motion
options.B: They never cost anything to run
options.C: They can't be targeted by interest

questions.explanation: They can show products in motion. Online video ads can show how a product works, using motion, sound and demonstrations that a printed newspaper ad can't provide. Video ads do cost money to produce and run, they reach people of many ages, often younger audiences than newspapers, and they can usually be targeted by interests, location and other factors. Many businesses use both media, choosing newspapers for local audiences who read them regularly and online video to show products to people who browse on their phones.

performanceIndicator.text: Explain types of advertising media

questions.question: Eggs labeled "Grade AA" have been judged against government standards for
questions.explanation: Quality. Grades rate products based on quality standards, such as the firmness of an egg white and the shape of its shell. The USDA's grading system tells consumers that Grade AA eggs meet the highest quality level. Grades don't set prices, though higher grades often sell for more, and they aren't about advertising or the color of the package. Grades help consumers compare products quickly and help businesses buy and sell in large quantities without inspecting every item.

performanceIndicator.text: Describe the uses of grades and standards in marketing

questions.question: A local hardware store wants to reach homeowners while they are driving to work. The best advertising medium for this goal is
questions.explanation: Radio. Radio reaches people while they drive, and local stations let a store target listeners in its own area at relatively low cost. A national magazine reaches readers across the country, most of whom can't visit the store, a trade journal targets professionals in a specific industry, and a printed catalog is read at home rather than during a commute. Matching the medium to where and when the target audience can be reached is one of the most important decisions in planning advertising.

performanceIndicator.text: Explain types of advertising media

questions.question: A company discovers that a battery used in its children's tablet can overheat if charged overnight. Fixing the problem will delay the holiday launch by two months. Which of the following is the most ethical decision:

options.A: Launch on time and hope no one notices
options.B: Launch on time with a small warning sticker
options.C: Sell the tablets only in other countries
options.D: Delay the launch until the battery is fixed

questions.explanation: Delay the launch until the battery is fixed. Ethical product management puts customer safety first, especially for products used by children. Delaying the launch until the battery is fixed prevents possible fires and injuries, even though the company loses holiday sales. Launching on time and hoping no one notices knowingly puts children at risk, a small sticker doesn't fix a known safety defect, and selling the tablets abroad would simply move the danger to other customers. Companies that knowingly sell unsafe products can also face recalls, lawsuits and lasting damage to their reputation.

performanceIndicator.text: Explain business ethics in product/service management

questions.question: A grocery chain wants to know whether playing slower music in its stores causes shoppers to spend more. It plays slow music in 10 stores and normal music in 10 similar stores for a month and compares sales. Which type of research design is this?
questions.explanation: Causal research. Causal research tests whether a change in one variable causes a change in another. By changing only the music in some stores and comparing sales with similar stores, the chain can judge whether music affects spending. Descriptive research describes characteristics without testing cause, exploratory research gathers early insights to define a problem, and secondary research uses data someone else already collected. Using similar stores for both groups helps make sure the music, rather than location, explains any difference.

performanceIndicator.text: Describe methods used to design marketing research studies (i.e., descriptive, exploratory, and causal)

questions.question: During the growth stage of the product life cycle, marketers usually

options.A: stop all promotion of the product.
options.D: introduce the product for the first time.

questions.explanation: Build preference against rivals. In the growth stage, sales rise quickly and competitors enter the market with similar products. Marketers focus on building preference for their brand, often by improving features, expanding distribution and promoting what makes their product different. Stopping promotion would let competitors gain ground, the product was already introduced in the previous stage, and removing it from stores happens in the decline stage, if at all. Growth is often the most profitable stage, so companies invest heavily to win market share.

performanceIndicator.text: Identify the impact of product life cycles on marketing decisions

questions.question: Ashford Home Goods sells several product lines under its own company name. When one line receives poor reviews for quality, sales of its other lines also fall. What best explains this result?

options.B: Each product line has a separate owner
options.C: Poor reviews raise sales of other lines
options.D: The corporate brand links all its products

questions.explanation: The corporate brand links all its products. When products share a corporate brand name, customers associate them with one another, so problems with one line can make shoppers doubt the rest. That is a risk of corporate branding, while its benefit is that a trusted name helps every product. Customers clearly notice brand names, since sales of other lines fell. The lines share one owner, Ashford, and poor reviews don't usually raise sales. Companies with corporate brands often invest heavily in quality control because a single failure can affect their whole reputation.

performanceIndicator.text: Explain the nature of corporate branding

questions.question: A customer who commutes by bike is looking at a jacket with reflective strips. Which statement best turns this feature into a benefit for her?

options.C: "Drivers can see you more easily at night."
options.D: "The strips are made of special material."

questions.explanation: "Drivers can see you more easily at night." A benefit explains how a feature helps the customer. For someone who bikes, being more visible to drivers at night improves her safety, which is a strong reason to buy. Describing the material or when the strips were added repeats facts without explaining why they matter, and mentioning colors talks about a different feature entirely. Analyzing product information ahead of time helps salespeople match each feature to the needs of different customers, such as safety for cyclists or style for others.

performanceIndicator.text: Analyze product information to identify product features and benefits

questions.question: A sunscreen company's sales forecast for July predicted strong sales, but the month turned out to be unusually rainy, and sales came in 20% below the forecast. Why did actual sales most likely miss the forecast?

options.A: Forecasts can't predict every outside factor
options.C: The company should stop making forecasts

questions.explanation: Forecasts can't predict every outside factor. Sales forecasts are based on past data and expected conditions, but unexpected events, such as unusual weather, economic changes or a new competitor, can make actual results differ. Forecasts are estimates, not guarantees, so they are never always exact. Rain reduces sunscreen use rather than increasing it. Stopping forecasts would leave the company with no basis for planning production and inventory. Instead, companies update forecasts as new information arrives and plan for a range of possible outcomes.

performanceIndicator.text: Explain the nature of sales forecasts

questions.question: A salesperson tells a customer that a laptop weighs only 2.5 pounds. This statement describes a
questions.explanation: Feature. A feature is a fact about a product, such as its weight, size or materials. The benefit is what that feature does for the customer, such as making the laptop easy to carry between classes. A warranty is a promise to repair or replace a product, and an objection is a customer concern about buying. Salespeople are most persuasive when they connect each feature to a benefit the customer cares about, because customers buy what products will do for them, not just what the products are.

performanceIndicator.text: Analyze product information to identify product features and benefits

questions.question: A car company that advertises its vehicles as the safest in their class is positioning its products based on
questions.explanation: A key product attribute. Positioning creates a distinct image of a product compared with competitors. Focusing on safety, a specific product attribute, gives customers who value safety a clear reason to choose the brand. The company isn't positioning on price, its history or the size of its dealerships. Other common positioning bases include price, quality, use, user type and comparison with competitors. Effective positioning is believable: the company must be able to support its safety claims with test results or ratings.

performanceIndicator.text: Describe factors used by marketers to position products/services

questions.question: A researcher asks 300 shoppers to rate a new juice on a scale of 1 to 5 and then calculates that the average rating is 4.1. Which of the following data-processing steps did the researcher perform:
questions.explanation: Tabulating and analyzing. Tabulation counts and organizes responses, and analysis uses calculations such as averages to find meaning in the data. Calculating an average rating of 4.1 from 300 responses is an example of both. A sampling frame is the list from which a sample is chosen, a focus group is a small group discussion, and open-ended questions let respondents answer in their own words. Researchers often compare averages across groups, such as age ranges, to see whether different customers react differently.

performanceIndicator.text: Explain techniques for processing marketing data

questions.question: A research firm that sells survey participants' email addresses to advertisers without permission is violating
questions.explanation: Participants' privacy. Research participants trust that their personal information will be used only as promised. Selling email addresses without permission violates that trust and their privacy, and it may break privacy laws and industry codes of ethics. Copyright protects creative works, not contact information, pricing policies concern what the firm charges, and free speech involves expressing opinions without government interference. Ethical researchers explain how data will be used and protect participants' identities. Many research firms follow published codes of ethics that require informed consent.

performanceIndicator.text: Explain the role of ethics in marketing-information management

questions.question: A toy maker tests its products to meet federal safety standards for children's toys before selling them. What is the main benefit of meeting these standards?

options.A: The company can ignore customer complaints
options.B: The toys can be sold without packaging
options.C: Parents can trust the toys are safe
options.D: The toys will cost nothing to produce

questions.explanation: Parents can trust the toys are safe. Safety standards set minimum requirements for products, such as limits on small parts and certain chemicals in children's toys. Meeting them reassures parents and allows the toys to be sold legally in the United States. Standards don't remove the need for packaging, let a company ignore complaints or make products free to produce; testing actually adds cost. Many retailers refuse to stock toys that can't show proof of meeting safety standards, so compliance also affects where a product can be sold.

performanceIndicator.text: Describe the uses of grades and standards in marketing

questions.question: A food company that labels its snacks "all natural" even though they contain artificial flavors is acting
questions.explanation: Unethically. Product labels must be honest. Calling snacks "all natural" when they contain artificial flavors misleads customers who choose products based on ingredients, which is unethical and may violate labeling laws. The practice isn't efficient, competitive in a fair sense or responsible, even if it increases short-term sales. Customers who discover misleading labels often lose trust in the whole brand and may share their experience online. Honest labeling protects both customers and the company's reputation.

performanceIndicator.text: Explain business ethics in product/service management

questions.question: A cell phone case company's oldest design has seen falling sales for two years as newer phone models replace the one it fits. Several retailers have already moved the case to their clearance shelves. Which marketing decision best matches this product's life cycle stage?

options.A: Raise its price to the highest level
options.B: Reduce support and plan to phase it out

questions.explanation: Reduce support and plan to phase it out. Falling sales over a long period as the phone it fits disappears shows the product is in the decline stage. Companies usually reduce spending on declining products and plan to phase them out, sometimes selling remaining stock at lower prices. Spending more on mass advertising rarely revives a product whose market is disappearing, raising the price would speed the decline, and introducing it to new customers doesn't make sense when fewer people own the phone. Resources are better spent on cases for newer models.

performanceIndicator.text: Identify the impact of product life cycles on marketing decisions

questions.question: A company planning a big promotion for a new cereal should first make sure that

options.C: stores will have the cereal in stock.
options.D: the ads run only after the sale ends.

questions.explanation: Stores will have the cereal in stock. Channel management and promotion must work together. If ads convince shoppers to look for the cereal but stores don't have it, the company wastes its advertising money and frustrates customers, who may buy a competitor's product instead. Price cuts at every store aren't required for a promotion, keeping the recipe secret has nothing to do with distribution, and running ads after the sale ends would defeat their purpose. Companies often confirm shipments to retailers weeks before a campaign begins.

performanceIndicator.text: Coordinate channel management with other marketing activities

questions.question: A new yoga studio gives free classes to several well-known local fitness instructors, hoping they will tell their students about the studio. Which of the following best describes this strategy:
questions.explanation: Using trusted local voices. The studio is using word of mouth by reaching people whose recommendations are trusted by its target audience. Fitness instructors already have students who value their opinions, so a positive mention can bring in new members at little cost. The strategy doesn't involve television ads, permanently lower prices or door-to-door selling. Word-of-mouth strategies like this work best when the product truly impresses the people chosen, because a disappointing experience can spread just as quickly.

performanceIndicator.text: Describe word-of-mouth channels used to communicate with targeted audiences

questions.question: Two coffee shops on the same street offer similar coffee at similar prices. One begins promoting itself as a quiet place for students to study, with long hours and free charging stations. What is this shop doing?

options.C: Positioning for a specific user group

questions.explanation: Positioning for a specific user group. Positioning by user means creating an image of the product as the best choice for a particular type of customer. By emphasizing quiet space, long hours and charging stations, the shop sets itself apart as the place for students. It hasn't changed prices, it is creating a different position rather than copying its competitor, and it still sells through the same store. Positioning matters most when competing products are similar, because the image in customers' minds becomes the main difference.

performanceIndicator.text: Describe factors used by marketers to position products/services

questions.question: A company that encourages satisfied customers to post reviews on independent review sites is using
questions.explanation: Word of mouth. Word-of-mouth promotion happens when customers share their experiences with others, in person or online. Reviews on independent sites are a modern form of word of mouth that many shoppers trust more than ads. Outdoor advertising includes billboards and signs, personal selling is direct communication between a salesperson and a customer, and trade promotions are offered to retailers and wholesalers. Companies can encourage reviews, but offering rewards only for positive reviews would be deceptive and may break rules.

performanceIndicator.text: Describe word-of-mouth channels used to communicate with targeted audiences

questions.question: A clothing brand's online sales have dropped 15% over three months, and managers can't agree on why. Some blame a competitor's new line, while others think the website's recent redesign confused shoppers. Website data shows that visits are steady, but no one has looked at where shoppers leave the site, and the brand hasn't surveyed customers in over a year. Which of the following should the brand do first:

options.B: Conduct research to find the real cause
options.C: Cut prices on every item immediately
options.D: Redesign the website again right away

questions.explanation: Conduct research to find the real cause. When managers disagree about the cause of a problem, marketing research can provide facts, such as website analytics showing where shoppers leave and surveys asking why they bought elsewhere. Acting before understanding the cause risks wasting money. Cutting prices may not help if the redesign is the problem, another redesign may not help if the competitor is the cause, and giving up online sales is an extreme reaction. Research helps the brand choose the solution that matches the real problem.

performanceIndicator.text: Explain the nature of marketing research

questions.question: A store advertises "Everything 50% off!" in large letters, but the sale applies to only a few items, which is explained in tiny print at the bottom of the ad. Which of the following describes this practice:
questions.explanation: Potentially deceptive advertising. Advertising is deceptive when its overall impression misleads consumers, even if the fine print is technically accurate. A headline claiming everything is half off, when only a few items are, is likely to mislead shoppers, and the FTC and state agencies can take action against such ads. Comparative advertising compares a product with competitors, institutional advertising promotes a company's image, and cooperative advertising is shared between manufacturers and retailers. Clear, honest claims protect a business's reputation and keep it out of legal trouble.

performanceIndicator.text: Describe the regulation of promotion

questions.question: A sporting goods store expects to sell 1,200 bicycles next spring based on past sales and local trends. This estimate is a
questions.explanation: Sales forecast. A sales forecast estimates how much a business expects to sell during a future period. The store bases its forecast on past sales and local trends, such as new bike trails in the area. A sales quota is a target assigned to a salesperson or team, a marketing budget plans spending on marketing, and a price list shows what products cost. Forecasts guide decisions about inventory, staffing and promotions, so the store can order enough bikes without being stuck with too many.

performanceIndicator.text: Explain the nature of sales forecasts

questions.question: A clothing retailer's email software automatically sends a discount code to customers on their birthdays. This is an example of technology that helps promotion by

options.D: raising the price of every item.

questions.explanation: Personalizing messages at scale. Email marketing software can use customer data, such as birthdays, to send personalized messages automatically to thousands of people, something that would be impossible to do by hand. Personalized offers often get more attention and sales than generic ones. The technology doesn't replace products, raise prices or limit online shopping. Businesses must also respect privacy rules and let customers unsubscribe from promotional emails, which is required by federal law. Companies that skip screening often spend heavily on ideas that never had a real market.

performanceIndicator.text: Describe the use of technology in the promotion function

questions.question: A smartphone maker surveys 1,000 users before designing its next model to find out which features matter most to them. This activity is
questions.explanation: Marketing research. Marketing research gathers and analyzes information to help solve marketing problems and guide decisions, such as which features to include in a new phone. Personal selling is direct communication with customers to make sales, channel management concerns how products reach customers, and pricing sets what customers pay. Research before product design helps companies avoid spending millions developing features that customers don't value, while finding ones they do. Researchers often start with existing sales and website data before collecting new data.

performanceIndicator.text: Explain the nature of marketing research

questions.question: A snack company asks customers on social media to suggest new flavors and receives thousands of ideas. This method of generating product ideas is
questions.explanation: Crowdsourcing. Crowdsourcing gathers ideas from a large group of people, often online. Customers know what they would like to buy, so their suggestions can reveal flavors the company hadn't considered. Test marketing tries a finished product in a limited area, commercialization is the full launch of a new product, and market saturation means most potential customers already own the product. Companies that crowdsource ideas still screen them carefully, because many suggestions won't be practical or profitable.

performanceIndicator.text: Identify methods/techniques to generate a product idea

questions.question: A gas station that raises prices sharply right after a hurricane, when customers have no other options, may be guilty of
questions.explanation: Price gouging. Price gouging means raising prices to unfair levels for essential goods during emergencies, when customers have few choices. Many states have laws against it. Penetration pricing sets low prices to enter a market quickly, psychological pricing uses prices such as $9.99 to influence perception, and prestige pricing sets high prices to suggest quality. Businesses that gouge customers during disasters may face fines and lasting damage to their reputation in the community. Many states activate price-gouging laws automatically when an emergency is declared.

performanceIndicator.text: Describe the role of business ethics in pricing

questions.question: Under federal rules, a social media influencer who is paid to promote a product must
questions.explanation: Clearly disclose the payment. The Federal Trade Commission requires influencers to clearly disclose when they are paid or receive free products in exchange for promotion, using labels such as "#ad" or "sponsored." This lets followers judge the endorsement fairly. Influencers aren't required to post only positive reviews, and requiring that would make endorsements less honest. Promotion naturally mentions the product's name, and influencers don't need approval from followers. Brands can also be held responsible when influencers fail to disclose these relationships.

performanceIndicator.text: Describe the regulation of promotion

questions.question: After collecting 500 online surveys, a researcher removes responses from people who answered every question in under 20 seconds. This step is part of
questions.explanation: Editing the data. Editing data means reviewing responses for errors, missing answers and unreliable entries before analysis. Surveys completed far too quickly suggest that respondents didn't read the questions, so removing them improves data quality. Sampling chooses who will be surveyed, writing the questionnaire happens before data collection, and presenting findings comes at the end. Clean data matters because conclusions are only as reliable as the information they are based on. Some researchers also add trick questions to catch respondents who aren't reading carefully.

performanceIndicator.text: Explain techniques for processing marketing data

questions.question: Two rival furniture stores secretly agree to stop offering discounts so they can both keep prices high. Which of the following describes this practice:
questions.explanation: Illegal price fixing. Price fixing is an agreement among competitors to set prices or limit discounts instead of competing. It harms customers, who lose the benefit of competition, and it is illegal under U.S. antitrust laws. Bundle pricing sells products together for one price, competitive pricing sets prices based on what competitors charge independently, and markup pricing adds a percentage to cost. Competitors may watch each other's prices, but they may not agree on them. Penalties for price fixing can include large fines and even prison time.

performanceIndicator.text: Describe the role of business ethics in pricing

questions.question: A customer asks an electronics salesperson whether a TV can be returned if it doesn't fit his wall. The salesperson isn't sure of the policy but says, "Sure, no problem." Which of the following is the main risk of this response:

options.A: The customer will buy a smaller TV
options.B: He may promise something the store won't honor
options.C: The salesperson will earn a higher commission
options.D: The store will automatically lower its prices

questions.explanation: He may promise something the store won't honor. Salespeople must know their company's selling policies so they can give accurate answers. If the store doesn't accept returns for that reason, or charges a restocking fee, the customer will feel misled when he tries to return the TV, and the store may lose his trust or face a complaint. The answer has nothing to do with TV size, store prices or commission. When unsure, a salesperson should check the policy or ask a manager rather than guessing.

performanceIndicator.text: Explain company selling policies

questions.question: A store's policy of matching any local competitor's advertised price is an example of a
questions.explanation: Selling policy. Selling policies are company rules that guide how salespeople handle situations such as returns, discounts, price matching and payment options. A price-match policy tells employees when and how to lower a price for a customer. Production schedules plan manufacturing, hiring procedures guide recruitment and supplier contracts set terms with vendors. Clear selling policies help employees treat every customer consistently and fairly, and they help customers know what to expect. Policies are often printed on receipts or posted near registers.

performanceIndicator.text: Explain company selling policies

questions.question: A juice company targets health-conscious adults by selling organic juices in natural food stores at premium prices. This combination of a target market and marketing mix is the company's
questions.explanation: Marketing strategy. A marketing strategy combines a chosen target market with a marketing mix of product, price, place and promotion designed to appeal to that market. Here, the company matches organic products, premium prices and natural food stores to health-conscious adults. A mission statement describes the company's purpose, a sales forecast predicts future sales, and an organizational chart shows how jobs are arranged. When every part of the mix fits the target market, the strategy is more likely to succeed.

performanceIndicator.text: Explain the concept of marketing strategies

questions.question: A company that surveys customers to learn their ages, incomes and shopping habits is conducting
questions.explanation: Descriptive research. Descriptive research describes the characteristics of a market or group, such as who customers are and how they shop, often through surveys. Causal research tests whether one factor causes a change in another, usually through experiments, which makes experimental research a form of causal research. Exploratory research gathers preliminary information to define a problem or develop ideas. Descriptive research is the most common type, because businesses frequently need accurate profiles of their customers. Retailers often use descriptive research to decide where to open new stores.

performanceIndicator.text: Describe methods used to design marketing research studies (i.e., descriptive, exploratory, and causal)

questions.question: A corporate brand differs from a product brand because it represents

options.A: the price of one specific product.
options.B: the package design of a single item.

questions.explanation: The whole company's reputation. A corporate brand is the image and reputation of the company as a whole, such as how people view its values, quality and behavior. Product brands identify individual products sold by the company. The price of a product, the design of its package and a short-term promotion are marketing elements, not the company's overall identity. A strong corporate brand can help every product the company sells, while a scandal involving the company can hurt all of its products at once.

performanceIndicator.text: Explain the nature of corporate branding

questions.question: Which of the following is necessary for a group of people to be considered a market for a product:

options.A: They want it and can afford to buy it
options.B: They have already bought the product
options.C: They are all the same age
options.D: They live in the same city as the business

questions.explanation: They want it and can afford to buy it. A market consists of people or organizations who have a need or want for a product and the ability and willingness to buy it. People who want something but can't afford it, or who can afford it but have no interest, aren't part of the market. Living near the business, being the same age and having already purchased aren't required. Businesses measure markets this way to decide whether enough potential buyers exist to justify launching or promoting a product.

performanceIndicator.text: Explain the concept of market and market identification

questions.question: A shoe brand has posted about 120 times on social media over the past six months. Its dashboard shows that posts featuring customer photos get three times more engagement than posts showing products alone. How should the brand use this information?

options.A: Stop posting on social media entirely
options.B: Remove all product photos from its website
options.D: Feature more customer photos in future posts

questions.explanation: Feature more customer photos in future posts. Social media analytics show which content audiences respond to most, and the data clearly favors customer photos. Featuring more of them is a data-driven way to improve results. Stopping social media posts would give up a channel that is clearly working, removing product photos from the website ignores that shoppers still need to see the products, and deleting posts that get comments would remove the very engagement the brand wants. Testing and adjusting content based on data is one of technology's biggest benefits for promotion.

performanceIndicator.text: Describe the use of technology in the promotion function

questions.question: A budget hotel chain wants to attract road-tripping families. Which of the following decisions best fits that marketing strategy:

options.D: Opening hotels only in city centers

questions.explanation: Locating hotels near major highways. A marketing strategy works when every decision fits the target market. Road-tripping families need convenient stops along their routes, so locating hotels near major highways matches their needs. City-center locations suit business travelers and tourists without cars, removing family rooms ignores the target market's needs, and luxury magazines reach wealthy readers rather than budget-conscious families. Strategies often fail not because of one bad idea but because product, price, place and promotion don't work together.

performanceIndicator.text: Explain the concept of marketing strategies

questions.question: Which of the following is the main purpose of screening new product ideas after brainstorming:

options.A: To drop ideas unlikely to succeed
options.B: To generate as many ideas as possible
options.C: To set the final retail price
options.D: To launch every idea at once

questions.explanation: To drop ideas unlikely to succeed. Brainstorming produces many ideas, but most won't be practical or profitable, so screening evaluates them against criteria such as customer need, cost and fit with the company's goals. Weak ideas are dropped before the company spends money developing them. Generating as many ideas as possible is the purpose of brainstorming itself, launching every idea at once would waste resources, and setting the final price comes much later in development. Screening saves time and money by focusing effort on the strongest ideas.

performanceIndicator.text: Identify methods/techniques to generate a product idea

questions.question: An online store tracks the percentage of website visitors who make a purchase. This measure is the
questions.explanation: Conversion rate. The conversion rate shows how many visitors take a desired action, such as buying, out of all visitors. If 2,000 people visit and 60 buy, the conversion rate is 3%. Market share is a company's percentage of total industry sales, inventory turnover measures how quickly stock sells, and profit margin shows how much of each sales dollar is profit. Marketers monitor conversion rates closely because small improvements, such as a simpler checkout, can add large amounts of revenue.

performanceIndicator.text: Identify data monitored for marketing decision making

questions.question: A researcher who wants to survey a store's loyalty-program members chooses every 20th name from the member list. This method is
questions.explanation: Systematic sampling. Systematic sampling selects every nth person from a list after a starting point, such as every 20th member. Because names are chosen by a fixed rule, it is a type of probability sample when the list isn't arranged in a pattern. Convenience sampling uses whoever is easiest to reach, quota sampling fills set numbers of people from different groups, and judgment sampling relies on the researcher's choice of who seems typical. Systematic sampling is quick and simple when a complete list is available.

performanceIndicator.text: Discuss the nature of sampling plans (i.e., who, how many, how chosen)

questions.question: A clothing retailer uses sales data to learn that a jacket sells well in its northern stores but poorly in southern ones. This information helps the retailer

options.C: decide where to send its inventory.

questions.explanation: Decide where to send its inventory. Marketing data helps businesses make better decisions about products, prices, promotion and distribution. Knowing where the jacket sells lets the retailer send more to northern stores and less to southern ones, which reduces markdowns and lost sales. Manufacturing costs are set by suppliers, the board of directors is chosen by shareholders, and the employee handbook covers workplace policies. Without data, the retailer would have to guess, and guesses about inventory often lead to empty shelves in some stores and piles of unsold goods in others.

performanceIndicator.text: Describe the need for marketing data

questions.question: A streaming service notices that the number of subscribers who cancel each month has risen from 2% to 5% since it raised prices. Which data is the company monitoring?
questions.explanation: Customer churn rate. The churn rate measures the percentage of customers who stop using a service during a period. Rising churn after a price increase suggests that some subscribers don't see enough value at the new price. Advertising reach measures how many people see ads, production costs measure what it costs to create content, and website speed measures performance. Companies monitor churn because keeping existing customers usually costs less than attracting new ones, so a rising rate can signal a serious problem.

performanceIndicator.text: Identify data monitored for marketing decision making

questions.question: A company that sells high-end running shoes identifies serious runners who race at least four times a year as its
questions.explanation: Target market. A target market is the specific group of customers a business focuses on. Serious runners who race often are likely to value performance shoes and pay higher prices, so the company aims its products and promotions at them. The entire population includes everyone, a distribution channel is the path products take to customers, and a competitive advantage is what makes a business better than competitors. Identifying a target market lets a business spend its marketing budget where it is most likely to pay off.

performanceIndicator.text: Explain the concept of market and market identification

questions.question: A restaurant owner believes customers want more vegetarian dishes, but she isn't sure. Why should she gather marketing data before changing the menu?

options.A: To avoid serving any vegetarian dishes
options.B: To guarantee every new dish succeeds
options.C: To delay the decision for several years
options.D: To base the decision on real evidence

questions.explanation: To base the decision on real evidence. Marketing data, such as customer surveys, sales of current vegetarian items and trends in the area, helps the owner learn whether her belief is correct and how many dishes to add. Basing decisions on evidence reduces risk. Gathering data isn't meant to rule out vegetarian dishes or delay the decision for years, and no amount of data can guarantee success. It can, however, make success much more likely and help her avoid spending money on menu changes customers don't want.

performanceIndicator.text: Describe the need for marketing data

questions.question: A company that sells its products through its own website and also through department stores is using
questions.explanation: Multiple channels of distribution. Using more than one route to reach customers, such as a company website and department stores, is called a multichannel strategy. It lets the company reach shoppers who prefer to buy online as well as those who want to see products in person. A single direct channel would mean selling only to consumers without intermediaries, a franchise system licenses independent owners to run branded businesses, and vertical price fixing is an illegal agreement on resale prices. Multiple channels can increase sales but require careful coordination to avoid conflict.

performanceIndicator.text: Explain the nature of channels of distribution

questions.question: A phone company surveys 50 customers in one mall about its service and uses the results to describe all of its 2 million customers nationwide. Which of the following is the main problem with this sampling plan:

options.A: The sample is too small and unrepresentative
options.B: The company has too many customers
options.C: The survey asked about the company's service

questions.explanation: The sample is too small and unrepresentative. A good sampling plan decides who to survey, how many and how to choose them so the sample represents the whole population. Fifty people at one mall are too few and too similar, since they all live near one location and shop at that mall, to describe 2 million customers across the country. Asking about service is the purpose of the survey, in-person surveys can be valid, and a large customer base simply requires a better sample. A larger random sample from the full customer list would give more reliable results.

performanceIndicator.text: Discuss the nature of sampling plans (i.e., who, how many, how chosen)
